sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *siempre que* + subjunctive "provided that, as long as" from B1 Unit 21 (*Apoyo la medida siempre que sea justa*). The same words have a second meaning: "whenever, every time". Then the verb is a fact that repeats, in the present or the past, so it takes the indicative. One expression, two meanings, and the mood tells you which one you have.

sections.title: Siempre que: two meanings
rows: Siempre que llueve, me quedo en casa.
Whenever it rains, I stay at home. (A habit: indicative.)
Siempre que llovía, me quedaba en casa.
Whenever it rained, I stayed at home. (A past habit: indicative.)
Salgo mañana siempre que no llueva.
I'll go out tomorrow provided it doesn't rain. (A condition: subjunctive.)
Cada vez que llueve, me quedo en casa.
Every time it rains, I stay at home. (Same habit, with *cada vez que*.)

sections.title: Cada vez que
sections.content: *Cada vez que* "every time" always counts repetitions. It follows the rule of *cuando*: indicative for habits and past events (*Cada vez que llamo, contesta*), subjunctive when it looks ahead to repetitions that have not happened yet (*Cada vez que necesites ayuda, llámame*). Unlike *siempre que*, it never means "provided that".

items.spanish: Siempre que hay tormenta, se va la luz.
items.english: Whenever there is a storm, the power goes out.

items.spanish: Siempre que visitaba a mi abuela, me preparaba chocolate caliente.
items.english: Whenever I visited my grandmother, she made me hot chocolate.

items.spanish: Te presto el carro siempre que me avises antes.
items.english: I'll lend you the car provided you tell me beforehand.

items.spanish: Cada vez que necesites ayuda, llámame.
items.english: Every time you need help, call me.

sections.content: A quick test: replace *siempre que* with *cada vez que*. If the sentence still works, it means "whenever" and takes the indicative. If it only works with *con tal de que* (B1 Unit 21), it means "provided that" and takes the subjunctive.
